How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Validation studies of zero-shot language-model scoring of psychological interviews often rely primarily on a single convergent correlation with a questionnaire to establish validity. However, a bivariate correlation cannot reveal whether a model lacks discriminant validity, agrees poorly in absolute terms, produces non-random missing scores, or scores inconsistently. We evaluated eight open-weight families (1-70B active parameters) and eight commercial frontier models. The models scored the same sets of clinical interviews (Study 1: suicide recovery, 𝑛 = 149; Study 2: future self-continuity, 𝑛 = 164) across 52 configurations. Convergent validity improves with model size in both studies. However, the standard open-weight models tested achieve only about three-quarters of frontier convergent validity, with 11-fold greater mean absolute bias, more format failures, and lower repeatability in Study 1. In Study 2, standard open models (≤ 27B) are as strongly correlated with a closely related construct (suicide recovery) as with the target (mean difference -0.014), although they correlate less strongly with a distal neighbor (life satisfaction). All six frontier generations correlate more strongly with the target than with either neighbor (mean difference from recovery +0.117). On a local workstation, Gemma 4 31B is within the frontier range on all discriminant validity indices, outperforming its similar-sized predecessor. Llama 3.3 70B shows no greater discriminant validity than Gemma 4 31B, suggesting that discriminant validity is a function of release, not parameter count alone. Based on these findings, we suggest a minimum validation standard across five domains.

Introduction

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have made it possible to automatically score open-ended psychological interviews. Specifically, a model can take a verbatim transcript of an interview and a set of natural-language instructions describing how to score the interview, without any training examples (i.e., zero-shot), and output a numerical rating of a psychological construct. LLM ratings of interviews and other open-ended text have been shown to correlate with validated measures of personality (Wright et al., 2026), life satisfaction (Mesquiti et al., 2026), spirituality (Prinzing et al., 2025), depression (Ohse et al., 2024), and clinician-rated symptom severity in people at clinical high risk for psychosis (Chen et al., 2026; but see Teferra et al., 2026, for posttraumatic stress symptoms; for discussion, see Abdurahman et al., 2024; Demszky et al., 2023). This method differs from previous word-list and supervised methods (Pennebaker et al., 2015) in that it only requires the rubric used by human raters, not any training examples (Ziems et al., 2024). This method has been applied to psychotherapy sessions (Eberhardt et al., 2025) and to psychiatric interviews, with a few scored examples added to the prompt (Girard et al., 2026), and in suicide research to create measures of future self-continuity (FSC; Sokol & Goodman, 2026) and recovery after a suicidal episode (Sokol et al., 2026).

In most cases, validity evidence consists of a single statistic: a convergent correlation between the model's score and a source questionnaire, or agreement with a human rating (Törnberg, 2024). When researchers compare different models, they typically rank them based on this statistic, assuming that the model with the higher correlation is the better measure (Girard et al., 2026). Some studies have also reported internal consistency, factor structure, or correlations with outcomes (Eberhardt et al., 2025; Wright et al., 2026). Others have labeled multiple constructs within the same design (Ziems et al., 2024) or examined discriminant validity with supervised language models (Gu et al., 2026; Oltmanns et al., 2026). Low et al. (2026) recently proposed a broader framework for evaluating the psychometric properties of textderived psychological measures, including content validity, construct validity, and reliability.

They showed that methods with good criterion validity can still miss prototypical expressions of the intended construct, so a single performance statistic can hide important measurement problems. However, we found no psychological measure, scored zero-shot by an LLM, that has been evaluated with a formal discriminant comparison against a neighboring questionnaire or a check of first-attempt scoring failures, and few that have been evaluated for limits of agreement or repeatability (Pimentel & Meyer, 2026; Sokol & Goodman, 2026).

A single correlation has never been sufficient evidence of validity (Loevinger, 1957; Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994). Construct validity requires that a measure of a construct not only correlate with measures of the same construct (convergent validity), but also be distinguishable from measures of neighboring constructs (discriminant validity; Campbell & Fiske, 1959; Cronbach & Meehl, 1955; Messick, 1995). The discriminant requirement is a routine part of questionnaire validation (Clark & Watson, 2019), but is seldom applied to model-derived scores.

For example, in the field of automated text analysis, researchers have used the presence of firstperson singular pronouns ("I-talk") as an indicator of depression, based on bivariate associations between the two variables. Only recently have discriminant tests been run, indicating that "I-talk" is a marker of general negative emotionality, not just depression (Tackman et al., 2019).

A convergent correlation does not tell us anything about these four properties. First, poor discriminant validity: A model instructed to score Construct A may nonetheless produce scores that correlate just as strongly with Construct B, either because the model fails to distinguish the intended construct from a neighboring one or because its scores reflect a broader feature of the participant or the interview (e.g., general distress, narrative coherence, interview length). Second, poor absolute agreement: A model may produce scores that correlate strongly with a self-report scale, but each score differs from the self-report scale by a scale point. While the strength of association is unchanged (Pearson's 𝑟), the model's scores cannot be interpreted in terms of the cutoffs of the scale. Third, non-random missing scores: When a model fails to produce a usable score, the case is typically excluded from analysis. If these failures are not random, however, they effectively determine the analytic sample (Rubin, 1976). Fourth, poor repeatability: Because models produce responses stochastically, a smaller model's lower validity may be due to its own response variability just as much as to less accurate scoring. Only repeated independent scoring passes can distinguish between these two possibilities. The lack of attention to such properties has had consequences in suicide research, where, for many years, published summary statistics failed to indicate how poorly prediction models performed in practice (Belsher et al., 2019).

Researchers with sensitive transcripts face a second challenge. Outsource scoring to a commercial provider and researchers risk violating confidentiality and data agreements, as well as institutional data security and review requirements (European Union, 2016; Marks & Haupt, 2023). In response to these and other concerns, researchers have expressed a desire for openweight models that they can run on their own machines (Girard et al., 2026; Palmer et al., 2024; Riedemann et al., 2024; Wiest et al., 2024). In addition to the ethical considerations, open-weight models are also more cost-effective per transcript. However, there is a lack of evidence to guide researchers in selecting the best local model. Brickman et al.'s (2025) recently published methodological guide for LLM-based psychological assessment lists criteria for model selection but offers no evidence on how to choose among models. In studies that compare multiple models, researchers have varied the prompt, sampling settings, or the platform used to run each model, in addition to the model itself (e.g., Alizadeh et al., 2025), so the model's own contribution cannot be isolated. Other studies have shown that performance on text classification tasks improves across successive model versions (Rathje et al., 2024) and with size within one model family (Ziems et al., 2024), but none have specifically assessed which psychometric properties improve with size.

The Present Research

The review above leaves us with two questions: What does a single convergent correlation tell us about a language-model measure? And what model should researchers with sensitive transcripts choose? Both these questions can be answered by a single experiment that only varies the scoring model and assesses models on those properties for which a criterion correlation alone is not informative. We conducted such an experiment for two measures, described below, using a range of open-weight models of varying size, and comparing them to commercial frontier models. In Study 2, we used two additional questionnaires, one assessing a construct that is proximal to the target (the proximal neighbor, suicide recovery), and one that is more distal (the distal neighbor, life satisfaction), to test whether the models' scores reflect the target construct rather than a neighboring one.

We address four questions. First, does convergent validity increase with model size, and does the relation replicate across constructs? Second, if open-weight and frontier models' scores are similarly correlated with a questionnaire, do the models differ in calibration, scoring failures, and repeatability? Third, if a model passes the convergent criterion, does it actually measure the construct it is named after, and does the answer change with model size? The distal neighbor test addresses the question of whether a model's scores measure the construct at all. The proximal neighbor test is a more challenging version of this test. Finally, what should a validation report for an LLM-derived measure include?

Method

In both studies, we transcribed and scored clinical interviews zero-shot and compared the scores to validated self-report criteria. All aspects of the interviews, including the prompt formatting and criteria, were held constant across all model configurations (cells) tested (Table 1; Supplement S1). Among the open cells, only the scoring model differed; the frontier scores came from the provider's own software, with its own system prompt and sampling settings (Supplement S6.1). We tested 52 model configurations across the two studies, as well as the extension study, and scored eight open cells (seven releases and one precision variant) in both studies. Note. Rows are grouped by developer; the text counts eight families (Gemma 3, Gemma 4, Granite 4, Llama 3.3, Ministral 3, Mistral, Qwen 3, Qwen 3.5). Full specifications are in Supplement S1. The nine models of the marketplace comparison are not counted (Supplement S6.2).

Models fall into two classes: open-weight models, which can be run on hardware controlled by the investigator, and frontier models, the reference class, which are the most powerful models currently available, and can only be accessed via an interface provided by the model vendor. For open models, we measure model size in terms of the number of parameters actively used, since many model versions only activate a subset of their parameters for each query (Supplement S1). This parameter count is confounded with other factors such as training data, architecture, pre-training date, and post-training alignment, but these are held relatively constant when comparing within a model family.

Study 1: Suicide Recovery (RESST) Corpus and Clinical Sample

The corpus comprised 224 recovery-interview recordings from 150 participants, collected at three waves (𝑛 = 108,71, and 45 recordings) of a longitudinal cohort study examining recovery after a suicidal episode. Participants were recruited online and screened in two stages (Supplement S3; Sokol et al., 2026). At each wave, they were asked to provide audio recordings of their responses to 15 standardized recovery prompts (average recording length = 33 minutes).

Recording was optional and was offered again at each wave, so 42 of the 150 participants made their first recording at the second or third wave. The recordings were transcribed using Whisper (Radford et al., 2023), and sample selection, audio quality control, and transcript verification procedures are detailed in Sokol et al. (2026). A single recording that was unscorable by all models was removed from validity analyses, but included in counts of scoring failures (224 requests per cell). Participants consented to their de-identified transcripts being analyzed computationally and cloud-hosted (see Ethics Approval).

Validity, calibration, and repeatability analyses were conducted using data from the first recording of each participant (𝑛 = 149, after excluding one participant whose only recording was unscorable), of whom 74% reported at least one lifetime suicide attempt (demographics in Supplement S3). The number of participants included was determined solely by the number of available recordings; no power calculation was performed.

Criterion Measure

The convergent criterion was the concurrent self-report total of the Recovery Evaluation and Suicide Support Tool (RESST), a 21-item, 1-5 measure of psychological suicide recovery based on the COURAGE model of recovery (Sokol et al., 2022) and validated in a recent study (Sokol et al., 2023).

Scoring Procedure and Configurations

All cells were given the recovery rubric (recovery_instructions_v3.txt) verbatim, without any example transcript or instructions for tuning the rubric to specific transcripts. The rubric (Supplement S2.1) included anchored 1-5 scales for overall recovery, four subscales, and instructions to provide a final line with the five scores in JSON, a machine-readable format. We kept the formatting identical across all cells, as models' performance can vary greatly with formatting (Sclar et al., 2023).

The 30 open cells described in this work are 24 releases from seven families and six precision cells (Ministral 3 re-run at 8-bit and 16-bit precision; Supplement S6.3). The size analyses described below are based on the 19 standard cells, which are 4-bit (Q4_K_M), instruction-tuned, and have at least 150 scorable transcripts. The remaining 11 cells are each different in one aspect (see Supplement S1 for details).

The four Claude models of the instrument validation study (Sokol et al., 2026), used here as the frontier reference, were Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5 (Anthropic, 2026a-d).

We re-used the scores reported by these models, which were generated using Claude Code,

Anthropic's command-line tool (see Supplement S6.1 for details on the software used, which differs from that of the open cells). Claude Code returns scores in a structured-output schema, rather than as parsed free text, and therefore frontier cells are not included in the audit of scoring failures. Software All open models tested in both studies were run on a single cloud-hosted NVIDIA A100 using Ollama (versions, sampling settings, and truncation check in Supplement S6.1). In addition, we tested uncontrolled software settings by scoring nine open models through commercial thirdparty hosts in a separate marketplace comparison (Supplement S6.2). Study 2: Future Self-Continuity (FSC) Corpus and Replication Sample Data for Study 2 come from the sample of Sokol and Goodman (2026; scores publicly available at OSF: 10.17605/OSF.IO/JC86M). The sample comprises 164 verbatim transcripts of open-ended interviews about the future self. Participants were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk and screened by CloudResearch (demographics in Supplement S4). This sample is mixed-risk, with 19.5% reporting a lifetime suicide attempt and 56.7% reporting pastyear suicidal ideation (Sokol et al., 2025). All 164 transcripts were used in this study.

Criterion Measures and Graded Nomological Battery

The convergent criterion was the total score on the Future Self-Continuity Questionnaire (FSCQ; Sokol & Serper, 2020). The FSCQ is a 1-6 self-report measure of the vividness, similarity, and positive affect that individuals feel toward their future self (Hershfield, 2011); higher scores indicate greater future self-continuity.

The full-scale reliability of the FSCQ is estimated to be 𝛼 = .81 (Han et al., 2025). The FSCQ was administered in the same session as the RESST (Sokol et al., 2023) and the 5-item Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS; Diener et al., 1985; 𝛼 = .91 in this sample). The FSCQ correlates 𝑟 = .671 with the RESST (proximal neighbor) and 𝑟 = .420 with the SWLS (distal neighbor). The RESST and SWLS correlate 𝑟 = .650. The comparison with the RESST was planned prior to scoring the open cells; the comparison with the SWLS was added after.

Scoring Configurations and Frontier Generations

The published FSC rubric (fsc_instructions_json.txt) was given to the models zero-shot, with an additional instruction for the final line of JSON scores (Supplement S2.2). The eight open cells were scored on the same A100 and software setup as Study 1 (Supplement S6.1).

The frontier group consisted of the six successive Claude versions released from June 2024 to July 2026 (scoring sources in Supplement S1; one excluded scoring pass in Supplement S5.3).

Extension Study (ASUS Ascent GX10)

To test whether larger open models have better discriminant validity, we added an extension study on a local ASUS Ascent GX10 workstation (128 GB unified memory; ASUS, 2025; Supplement S7.1). First, we re-scored Gemma 3 12B and 27B on the GX10 and compared them to the A100 on three bridge criteria (Supplement S7.1). In advance, we set a rule that if any criterion was not met, cells from the GX10 would be reported separately and would not be pooled with A100 cells in any slope, group mean, or cross-study correlation. We then scored two models. Gemma 4 31B, the most valid open model of Study 1, was not scored in Study 2 because of computational constraints; it was scored here in two independent passes. Llama 3.3 70B, the largest model that could be run on the workstation, was scored in a single pass (model tags in Supplement S7.1).

Data Analysis

Convergent validity and model size. Convergent validity was assessed by computing the Pearson correlation (𝑟) with the target criterion. Where "validity" appears below without qualification, it refers to this coefficient. We regressed Fisher 𝑧-transformed correlations on log 10 active parameters and computed model-level and participant-level bootstrap intervals (2,000 replicates; Efron & Tibshirani, 1994). We tested the sensitivity of our findings to the choice of model family by conducting leave-one-family-out refits (Supplement S3).

Agreement. Bland-Altman mean bias (model minus criterion), standard deviation of differences, 95% limits of agreement (Bland & Altman, 1986 , 1999), proportion of mean squared difference attributable to constant bias, and proportional bias (regression of differences on means; definitions in Supplement S3) were calculated.

Scoring failures.

First-attempt responses that could not be scored were classified as format failures (i.e., no final line of scores could be read), truncations at the length limit, or explicit refusals. Across cells, we correlated analytic sample size with convergent validity (Rubin, 1976). For cells with at least five unscored participants, we compared criterion scores of scored and unscored participants (Welch's 𝑡; exploratory).

Repeatability.

Repeatability was indexed by the correlation between two complete scoring passes of a cell and by absolute agreement between the passes, ICC(A,1), the two-way intraclass correlation for absolute agreement of single scores (McGraw & Wong, 1996). The slope on model size was re-estimated based on correlations disattenuated for imperfect repeatability.

Discriminant validity.

The difference between the target and neighbor correlations (𝑟 target -𝑟 neighbor ), the target and neighbor partial correlations (the model score's partial correlation with the target controlling for the neighbor, and with the neighbor controlling for the target), and Williams's (1959) 𝑡-test for dependent correlations that share the model score, were used as discriminant validity indices. Even a measure of Construct A alone (a pure measure) will be correlated with a neighboring Construct B, because the two constructs share true variance.

Using attenuation theory, we calculated the expected differences and neighbor partials for a pure measure, assuming criterion reliabilities of . 80 to . 95 (Schmidt & Hunter, 1996; Spearman, 1904; Supplement S5.1).

Group inference.

Open and frontier groups were compared using Welch's (1947) 𝑡-test on Fisher 𝑧, with cells as units. Because all cells in Study 2 were scored for the same 164 transcripts, we also compared the two groups using a participant-level bootstrap (5,000 resamples; Supplement S5.2).

Use of generative AI. Claude (Anthropic) was used to write and check analysis code and to revise and edit manuscript text from the authors' content. It did not generate, simulate, or alter any data. The authors reviewed all output and take full responsibility for the manuscript.

Results

Results give the cell-level values for all 52 cells.

Study 1: Convergent Validity Across Model Sizes

Study 1: Three Issues Not Assessed by Criterion Correlation

Calibration. The open and frontier models differed primarily in their mean bias (Figure 2). Across the 19 standard open cells, the mean absolute bias of the open models was 0.508 points on the 1-5 metric, compared to 0.045 for the four frontier models (an 11.3-fold difference).

The mean width of the 95% limits of agreement was 3.10 points for open models, and 2.42 for frontier models (a 1.3-fold difference). The largest individual mean bias was seen for Qwen 3 4B (+1.03). Bias and scatter varied independently, and proportional bias was significant in 9 of 19 standard open cells (Supplement S3). Specifically, frontier models were more than a point off from the questionnaire for 8-13% of participants, whereas open cells were off for about 30%. Differ in Constant Bias, Not Scatter. Note. Filled diamonds designate frontier Claude models (𝑘 = 4); open circles designate standard open-weight configurations (𝑘 = 19). The vertical dashed Scoring failures varied across families, but not size. For example, Gemma 3 had 0.0 format failures per cell, while Granite 4 had 26.0. In fact, the worst cell (Granite 4 32B-A9B) had fewer than 150 usable scores (Supplement S3). Across open cells, we found that analytic sample size was positively correlated with convergent validity (Spearman 𝜌 = .58, 𝑝 = .001). In only one of 10 cells with five or more unscored participants (Granite 4 3B) did unscored participants have lower RESST scores than scored participants; in all other cells, the difference was not significant (Supplement S3.1).

Repeatability.

The seven rescored cells showed a monotonic increase in repeatability from 𝑟 = .676 (Granite 4 3B) to 𝑟 = .957 (Gemma 4 31B), with a Spearman correlation of 𝜌 = .991 between active parameters and repeatability. Absolute agreement between passes was as high as their correlation (ICC(A,1) = .670 to . 958), and on average the second pass differed from the first by at most 0.11 points (Supplement S3). Within these seven cells, differences in repeatability accounted for 20.2% of the slope on model size, a very rough estimate (95% CI [4.5%, 84.5%]; Supplement S3), with the remaining 79.8% accounted for by systematic differences in scoring.

Precision and reasoning variants. Quantization to 4 bits reduced validity at 3B and 8B, but not at 14B (combined one-tailed 𝑝 = .051), and there was no measurable drop in validity for any size when using 8-bit quantization. Reasoning-tuned variants did not score less validly (𝑝 = .174; Supplement S6.3, S6.4).

The Fisher-𝑧 slope was 𝑏 = 0.225 (95% CI [0.133, 0.365], 𝑃(slope ≤ 0) = .001; Table 2; Figure 1B). The open mean was 73.5% of the frontier mean (𝑀 = .400 vs. . 544). The validities of Study 1 and Study 2 correlated 𝑟 = .74 across the seven shared cells (Spearman 𝜌 = .64), with future self-continuity being scored with lower validity than recovery for each shared cell (Supplement S4). The seven standard open cells (≤ 27B) had a mean difference between their target and proximal-neighbor correlations (𝑟 FSCQ -𝑟 RESST ) of -0.014 (Figure 3). By Williams's test, none of the open cells' proximal differences were significant (Supplement S4). Frontier models were close to this expectation, while open models were well below it.

In an exploratory facet analysis, open and frontier models performed similarly on

Positivity, but less so on Similarity (open: 𝑀 = .20, frontier: 𝑀 = .47). The open models' overall score was highly correlated with their Positivity score (Supplement S5.4).

Extension Study: Larger Open Models on Local Hardware (ASUS GX10)

Gemma 3 27B passed all three bridge criteria, but Gemma 3 12B failed one (Supplement S7.2), so, as prespecified, the GX10 cells are reported separately.

Gemma 4 31B had an 𝑟 of . 525 and . 529 with the FSCQ on its two passes (repeatability 𝑟 = .955), as predicted from its model size (Supplement S7.3), and performed similarly to the lowest frontier generations. It was within the frontier range on all discriminant validity indices (Supplement S4), with proximal differences of +0.099 and +0.096, similar to Sonnet 5 (+.096).

Williams's test was not significant for Gemma 4 31B or the two 2026 frontier models (Supplement S4).

Llama 3.3 70B had an 𝑟 of . 470, which was lower than expected based on its size (though within the 95% prediction interval; Supplement S7.3), and lower than that of Gemma 3 12B, Gemma 3 27B, and Gemma 4 31B. Its proximal difference was +0.058 (Williams's 𝑝 = .301), which was smaller than expected for a pure measure (+0.076).

In the participant-level bootstrap, both models had larger proximal differences than the mean of the seven smaller open cells (Gemma 4 31B by . 112, 95% CI [.030, .208]; Llama 3.3 70B by . 072, [.005, .143]). Neither differed significantly from the frontier mean, and they did not differ from each other (Supplement S5.2). The fact that neither model's own difference excluded zero means that, as with the two 2026 frontier models, they are judged by their performance relative to other models in the group. On the same machine, Gemma 4 31B's proximal difference was larger than that of Gemma 3 27B, its predecessor model of nearly the same size, by . 097 (95% CI [.024, .173]; exploratory, Supplement S5.2). Llama 3.3 70B, more than twice the size of Gemma 4 31B, was intermediate between the smaller open cells and the frontier group. Both extension models exhibited the construct-level mean bias found in all models on this construct.

Discussion

Our goal was to answer two questions : (1) What does a single convergent correlation tell us about a language-model measure?

(2) What model should researchers with sensitive transcripts choose? The answer to the second question appears straightforward based on the typical evidence presented in this field. Convergent validity, as assessed by correlation with a criterion measure, clearly improves with model size, both across the open models and from the open models to the frontier models, whose sizes are not disclosed but are thought to be much larger. In fact, in both studies, the standard open-weight models achieved, on average, roughly three-quarters of the frontier's convergent validity. Thus, it appears that the decision comes down to cost. However, a convergent-only approach does not capture any of the properties that differentiate a valid measure from an invalid one with the same or a similar correlation. A more nuanced answer requires examining four further properties: whether the model distinguishes the target from neighboring constructs (discriminant validity), whether its scores agree with the scale in absolute terms (calibration), whether it produces a usable score for each case (scoring failures), and whether repeated scoring passes give consistent scores (repeatability). Regarding discriminant validity, the standard open models (all models with ≤ 27B parameters) do not differentiate between future self-continuity and suicide recovery, whereas the frontier generations do. Regarding calibration, in Study 1, the open and frontier models differed most in a correctable constant bias of up to a full scale point, which cannot be detected by 𝑟. Regarding scoring failures, in the worst cell, the model provided no valid score for one-third of the sample.

Finally, regarding repeatability, smaller models provided less consistent scores across repeated passes and, after correction for that inconsistency, still scored less validly.

Failure to Distinguish Neighboring Constructs and What Determines It

A convergent-only validation strategy, which focuses on the target alone, would have led researchers to conclude that all of the standard open models were valid, the error Campbell and Fiske (1959) warned against. The problem is not that the models are all inaccurate in their scoring of the target, since they are all able to discriminate between future self-continuity and life satisfaction, at least in terms of direction. The problem arose with the proximal neighbor, where these constructs are similar in that they both have narrative themes of future orientation, hope, and recovery. There are three non-mutually exclusive interpretations of these results, all of which should be treated as exploratory. First, the smaller models may be scoring a general impression of how well the person is doing, which is what both questionnaires are doing. When controlling for recovery, the smaller models' association with the target was about half that of the frontier models. Second, the failure may be specific to the facet that distinguishes the construct. The open models were able to score positive affect toward the future self about as validly as the frontier models, but they scored similarity between present and future self poorly. Their overall scores were strongly correlated with their Positivity scores, which is the subscale of future selfcontinuity most strongly related to recovery (FSCQ subscale correlations with the RESST:

Positive affect 𝑟 = .690, Similarity 𝑟 = .365; Supplement S5.4). A composite score can therefore correlate well with its criterion while the model fails on the facet that separates the target from its neighbor, so facet scores can show why good convergent validity does or does not come with good discriminant validity. Third, part of the failure may be due to characteristics of the material itself. In a mixed-risk sample, the interviews contain recovery content that a less discriminating model may include in its rating.

However, the extension study changed this interpretation. In fact, in our tests Gemma 4 31B fell within the observed frontier range on all discriminant validity indices, and its proximal difference did not differ significantly from the frontier mean. What set Gemma 4 31B apart from other models was not its size alone. Its predecessor, Gemma 3 27B, which is nearly as large, failed to distinguish the target from its proximal neighbor even on the same workstation.

Similarly, Llama 3.3 70B, more than twice as large as Gemma 4 31B, did not show greater discriminant validity. Discriminant validity is possible in a locally run model, but in these data it depended on the release, not on parameter count alone, and it only emerged in the largest models that a single workstation can run.

Calibration, Repeatability, and the Limits of the Measures

The issue of absolute calibration is particularly relevant when scores are compared to a threshold, as opposed to when scores are ranked. In Study 1, the open models were systematically higher than the frontier models, but their scatter was only modestly wider. This pattern can be removed with a calibration subsample: participants who are scored by both the model and the questionnaire. Since approximately half of the open cells showed proportional bias, a correction that accounts for both the intercept and the slope is necessary. All models, including frontier generations, rated participants higher for future self-continuity than the questionnaire. This bias is a property of the combination of rubric, interview, and questionnaire, and not of any particular model. Calibration does not, however, correct poor discriminant validity. A linear correction removes constant and proportional bias without changing the model's correlation with the target or with either neighbor, so a calibrated score can agree more closely with the questionnaire in absolute terms while still reflecting a broader or different construct.

Correcting for imperfect repeatability reduced the slope on model size by about a fifth (by an imprecise point estimate), but did not eliminate it. This suggests that scores from a single pass underestimate the validity a small model can achieve. Averaging repeated passes is an untested but inexpensive correction that can be used locally. It should be emphasized that repeatability differs from the reliability of a human rater. Rescoring reruns the same model in the same state, so repeatability reflects only the random variation in the model's own responses, which a lower temperature reduces. High repeatability therefore shows that a model scores consistently, not that it measures the construct (Gemma 4 31B in Study 1: repeatability 𝑟 = .957, convergent 𝑟 = .661).

There are two important limitations on how these measures can be used. First, none of the configurations examined here, including the frontier, were sufficiently similar to the questionnaire to allow them to be used as a replacement for the questionnaire for any individual.

Even the most valid models had approximately one in ten participants whose scores differed from their self-report by more than a full scale point. Second, the frontier series demonstrates that researchers cannot depend on newer models to provide increased validity. Over 25 months, six frontier generations of models were examined, and yet convergent validity of the selfcontinuity pairing remained largely unchanged. Newer model generations may improve in certain capacities while not improving in the validity of their rubric scoring. As new generations are released and general capacities improve, each needs to be reassessed for validity. It is likely that future increases in validity will be found through careful psychometric design of subscales, structured elicitation, and calibration subsamples, rather than merely through adopting a newer model.

Scoring Failures

The cells that failed to score transcripts were the less valid ones; therefore, the presence of unscored cases did not inflate the reported validity of any model. However, the risk is not just about individual cases. If failures are concentrated on ambiguous or atypical transcripts, they will determine the analytic sample (Rubin, 1976). In two cells, the participants that the model failed to score differed on the criterion from the ones it did score. Researchers should note and inspect all first-attempt failures, rather than ignore them or re-score them without recording the failure.

A Minimum Validation Standard

Current standards in psychology require validity evidence for every intended interpretation of a score (AERA, APA, & NCME, 2014; see also Lin, 2026). However, the field has not yet agreed on how this standard should be interpreted when the instrument under consideration combines a model, a rubric, and a software setup.

There are many opportunities for defensible choices in language-model measurement (model, precision, software setup, and prompt), and there are reporting standards for this kind of flexibility. Box 1 outlines a minimum standard of five evidence domains: one for the convergent evidence the field already reports, and one for each property that convergent evidence cannot detect. Within each domain, other analyses that answer the same question can replace those listed. This standard is the psychometric counterpart of two existing reporting standards: REFORMS, for machine-learningbased science (Kapoor et al., 2024), and TRIPOD-LLM, for reporting the processing steps, sampling settings included (Gallifant et al., 2025). In the vocabulary of questionable measurement practices (Flake & Fried, 2020), failure to report any domain in Box 1 is a practice to avoid. Two 2026 proposals complement this standard: Pimentel and Meyer (2026) validate a model as a replacement coder, and Girard et al. (2026) benchmark open-weight models with a fairness audit. However, neither tests discriminant validity or reports limits of agreement, both of which we view as essential.

The five domains in Box 1 are intended as a minimum for evaluating numerical scores derived from psychological interviews, rather than an exhaustive account of measurement quality. Box 1. Minimum validation evidence for an LLM-derived psychological measure 1. Convergent validity. Pearson and Spearman correlations with a validated criterion and, where possible, the same correlations for reference models scored on the same material. 2. Discriminant validity. Correlations with concurrently administered neighboring instruments; the difference between the target and neighbor correlations (𝑟 target -𝑟 neighbor ), Williams's test for dependent correlations, target and neighbor partial correlations, and comparison with the values expected for a pure measure, adjusted for attenuation. 3. Bland-Altman agreement. Mean bias, standard deviation of differences, 95% limits of agreement, the share of the mean squared difference due to constant bias, and a regression test for proportional bias. 4. Audit of first-attempt scoring failures. All initial failures from raw logs, classed as format failures, truncations, or refusals; the analytic sample size per model configuration; and a test of whether missingness relates to participant characteristics. 5. Repeatability. Consistency and absolute agreement (ICC(A,1)) across repeated independent scoring passes under operational settings, with validity reported both observed and disattenuated. High repeatability shows that the model scores consistently, not that its scores are valid.

Practical Recommendations

In this study, a 12B to 31B open-weight model was sufficient to achieve most of the frontier's convergent validity (65% to 96% of the frontier mean in Study 1), without the need for a third-party processor. Through a commercial marketplace, it cost roughly one-fortieth of the estimated per-transcript cost of a frontier model at July 2026 prices (Supplement S6.5).

When used in conjunction with the other recommendations in Box 1, this model can provide a valuable research tool. Models should be run on dedicated hardware with the model version, software version, context length, and temperature all fixed; when we ran open models through a commercial marketplace, the relation between model size and validity was eliminated. When a measure must discriminate between a target and a proximal clinical neighbor, researchers should not assume that a standard open model will suffice. In these data, the best-performing locally run configuration was Gemma 4 31B. Whatever model is chosen, researchers should test the difference between the target and neighbor correlations for the construct being measured rather than infer discriminant validity from the model's size or recency. Scores should be interpreted as absolute scores only after correction against a calibration subsample. With about 50 participants, a calibration subsample gives a standard error of the mean difference of about 0.15 points on a 5point scale; where proportional bias is present, the slope must be estimated as well, which needs a larger subsample. Investigators should check scoring failures on a subset of their sample before scoring the full sample. In cases where quantization may be preferred for practical reasons, it is noteworthy that in our studies eight-bit precision produced no detectable loss of validity at any size tested, and any loss of validity when using 4-bit precision was limited to the smallest models tested. Limitations This set of studies has six limitations. (1) In comparing released models, we cannot isolate the effects of active parameter count from other factors that influence performance, such as training data (Hoffmann et al., 2022), architecture, and alignment. Thus, cross-family comparisons should be interpreted as comparisons of releases, not families. (2) Our sample of 52 configurations is a purposive sample of prominent releases, so the relations between model size and validity characterize these releases, not all LLMs. Likewise, the open-versus-frontier comparisons concern the releases tested here, not two classes of models. (3) We tested discriminant validity for a single construct pair in a single sample. The open cells in Study 2 were not rescored, and therefore, their correlations are uncorrected for attenuation.

This means that while we demonstrate that failure can occur, we do not estimate its prevalence across clinical domains. In addition, the questionnaires served as criteria, not as true scores. A transcriptderived score may contain construct-relevant variance that a self-report questionnaire misses, so the validity estimated here is relative to these criteria and their expected relations. (4) Our frontier reference was a model family from a single provider, scored with different software than the open cells. (5) The extension study includes two models, one of which was scored in a single pass. Its results should be treated as tentative until replicated. We chose Gemma 4 31B as the most valid open model of Study 1 for use in the extension study. This choice could have overstated its convergent validity (though not its discriminant validity). ( 6) Every cell in our study uses the same transcription. Both transcription and model judgment have documented biases against minoritized speakers and dialects (Hofmann et al., 2024; Koenecke et al., 2020).

Relatedly, speech acoustics change with clinical severity (Cummins et al., 2015). Finally, we did not conduct a fairness audit of the kind Girard et al. (2026) describe; such an audit could partially test whether these biases moderate validity across demographic groups.

Conclusions

A measure can pass a commonly used convergent-validity check while failing on properties essential to its intended interpretation. Specifically, a model can correlate . 50 with its target questionnaire and just as strongly with a neighboring construct, increase or decrease each score by a scale point, not score certain types of cases, and give a different score on a second pass. The use of a convergent correlation would not detect any of these issues. This is not novel to psychometrics: Discriminating between a valid measure and an invalid measure with a similar correlation is standard practice that should be applied to our new LLM-based methods. This is often not challenging. Most of what is needed can be calculated from data that have already been collected, and the questionnaire needed for a discriminant test is often already part of the battery.

We hope that researchers will take these steps and report the five domains in Box 1 before adopting further automated measures.

S2. Scoring rubrics, verbatim

The text below is read directly from the files used in the scoring runs. The transcript was appended after the rubric in each request.

S2.

1 Study 1: recovery rubric (recovery_instructions_v3.txt) <background> This assessment measures personal recovery following a suicidal episode, as d efined by the Recovery Evaluation and Suicide Support Tool (RESST; Sokol et a l., 2023). Personal recovery is distinct from clinical recovery: it does not require the remission of symptoms or the absence of distress. Following Anthony (1993), it is "a way of living a satisfying, hopeful, and contributing life even with in the limitations caused by illness"-a deeply personal process of reclaiming agency, worth, connection, and meaning. A person can therefore be well into recovery while still describing pain, struggle, and difficult circumstances. You are scoring recovery-not symptom severity, suicide risk, likeability, or verbal fluency. Distressing content, inarticulate speech, or morally admirabl e behavior are not, in themselves, evidence in either direction. The transcript contains a participant's spoken answers to up to 15 open-ended prompts spanning the four domains below; some participants answered fewer th an 15. The RESST conceptualizes suicide personal recovery as a single global constru ct composed of four interrelated lower-order domains. Assess each domain on t he basis of what the transcript reveals about the person's current lived expe rience-both what they state explicitly and what is implicit in how they descr ibe themselves, their life, and their relationships: 1.

Self-Worth: A positive sense of self-identity. The degree to which the per son likes and accepts themselves (even when others do not accept them), trust s themselves, feels confident handling life's challenges, has learned to thin k about themselves in a more positive way, is proud of who they are becoming, and is able to forgive themselves.

2. Life Worth: Meaning and the desire to live. The degree to which the person experiences meaning and purpose, has something or someone worth living for, is willing to live, and feels that life is worth living even with its ups and downs.

3. Social Worth: Feeling accepted within meaningful relationships. The degree to which the person feels cared about, safe, connected, accepted, valued, an d respected within mutually respectful relationships-a sense of belonging and mattering to others. 2. Assign a score between 1 and 5 for each subcomponent (Self-Worth, Life Wor th, Social Worth, and Self-Understanding) and for overall recovery. Scores ma y include decimals (e.g., 3.5) to express placement between adjacent rubric a nchors.

3. Do not penalize a person for describing pain, struggle, or hard circumstan ces if they also convey genuine self-worth, meaning, connection, or self-unde rstanding. Withdrawal from relationships framed as not needing others is evid ence of limited, not strong, Social Worth.

4. If the transcript contains ambiguous, incomplete, or contradictory informa tion, use your best judgment to interpret the overall sense conveyed, weighin g the person's prevailing current experience over isolated or past statements.

5. If the transcript contains too little construct-relevant content to score (for example, the participant declines to answer, the recording is essentiall y empty, or the content does not address any of the prompts), do not estimate scores. Instead, state briefly why the transcript is unscoreable and output the insufficient-transcript JSON specified in the output format. A short tran script that nonetheless contains substantive construct-relevant content shoul d be scored.

6. Transcripts are automatic speech-to-text and may contain disfluencies, tra nscription errors, the participant reading the interview prompts aloud, or oc casionally the same passage duplicated by a recording artifact. Do not treat read-aloud prompt text as the participant's own narrative or count duplicated passages as additional evidence.

7. For each score, follow this process: a. Review the transcript as it relates to the construct and rubric b. Think step-by-step to develop an assessment c. Provide the numerical assessment 8. Use the rubrics provided below to guide your scoring.

</instructions> <rubrics> Self-Worth Rubric: 1: Self-worth absent or negative.

Dislikes or distrusts self, cannot accept o r forgive self, and expresses no pride in who they are.

2: Largely lacking self-worth. Little self-acceptance; struggles to trust or forgive self; self-view is mostly critical or contingent on others' approval.

3: Mixed or conditional self-regard. Some self-acceptance, self-trust, confid ence, and pride, but fragile, uneven, or contingent; self-forgiveness is diff icult and inconsistent.

4: Generally positive self-regard. Likes and accepts self (largely independen t of others' approval), trusts own judgment, feels confident handling challen ges, is usually able to forgive self, and takes pride in their growth, despit e some self-doubt.

5: Robust self-worth. Consistently likes, accepts, and trusts self; feels con fident and capable; forgives self; is proud of who they are becoming; and mai ntains this regard even when others do not affirm it.

Life Worth Rubric: 1: Sees little or no meaning or purpose; few or no reasons for living; ambiva lent, indifferent, or negative about being alive.

2: Tenuous sense of meaning and few reasons for living, though willingness to live is present even if fragile or newly re-established.

3: Some meaning and reasons for living, but inconsistent or conditional; the sense that life is worth living coexists with significant doubt or difficulty.

4: Clear sources of meaning and purpose and identifiable reasons for living; affirms that life is worth living through its ups and downs.

5: Strong, stable sense of meaning and purpose; firm reasons for living; clea rly values life and conveys a sense of actively choosing it.

Social Worth Rubric (weight the overall felt sense of belonging across the pe rson's relationships; one secure relationship amid otherwise absent or hurtfu l relationships typically indicates the middle of the scale, not the top): 1: Feeling cared for, safe, connected, or valued is absent from the person's account; relationships are missing, hostile, or harmful.

2: Minimal connection; doubts that others genuinely care; limited safety or s ense of being valued in relationships.

3: Some genuine connection and care, but inconsistent, partial, or uncertain; mixed sense of being valued, safe, and respected.

4: Generally feels cared about, safe, connected, accepted, and valued within meaningful, mutually respectful relationships, despite some remaining strain, distance, or unevenness.

5: Strong, secure sense of belonging across relationships; consistently feels deeply cared for, safe, valued, and connected within mutually respectful rel ationships.

Self-Understanding Rubric: 1: Self-understanding absent; confused by own reactions; fragmented or unclea r sense of who they are.

2: Limited insight; often confused or surprised by own reactions; weak cohere nce in their sense of self.

3: Moderate insight; understands some aspects of self, reactions, and behavio rs; partial coherence; some integration of past experiences.

4: Good self-understanding; aware of own strengths, challenges, and character istic thought and emotional patterns; a fairly coherent sense of self; connec ts current challenges to life history.

5: Deep, integrated self-understanding; clear grasp of strengths, challenges, and inner reactions; a coherent identity narrative that meaningfully situate s current challenges within one's life history.

Overall Recovery Rubric (a holistic judgment across the four domains, typical ly near their average; a markedly low single domain should lower, but not dom inate, the overall score): 1: Little to no sense of personal recovery.

Worthlessness or emptiness, life feeling not worth living, disconnection or isolation, and little self-underst anding.

2: Minimal or fragile recovery. Predominantly negative or depleted sense of s elf, tenuous reasons for living, weak or strained connection, and limited sel f-understanding.

3: Moderate, mixed recovery. Ambivalent or conditional self-worth, a sense th at life is worth living that is qualified or effortful, some meaningful conne ction, and partial self-understanding.

4: Considerable recovery. Generally positive sense of self, a clear sense tha t life is worth living, meaningful and supportive connection, and good self-u nderstanding, with some remaining struggles. The first 4,618 characters are identical to the published rubric (Sokol & Goodman, 2026); the closing instruction about the final line of JSON was added for this study.

<background> Future self-continuity (FSC) refers to the psychological connectedness people have with their future selves-the sense of persistence of selfhood from the present to the future. It represents the degree to which a person identifies their future self as being the same person as their current self.

FSC has three subcomponents: 1.

Similarity to the future self: How similar one's current self is to their future self in terms of beliefs, values, personality, and other aspects of id entity.

2. Vividness of the future self: How vividly an individual can imagine their future self and project themselves into the future. Similarity to Future Self Rubric: 1: Expects very little similarity between current and future self.

2: Anticipates a few similarities in minor aspects, but expects core identity to change.

3: Expects moderate similarity, with some core aspects remaining consistent a nd others changing.

4: Envisions considerable similarity, with most key aspects of identity remai ning continuous.

5: Anticipates high similarity, with beliefs, values, personality and identit y largely unchanged.

6: Expects very high similarity bordering on sameness between current and fut ure self.

Vividness of Future Self Rubric: 1: Has little to no ability to imagine or envision the future self.

Future se ems abstract and unreal.

2: Can imagine the future self to a minimal degree, but the image is vague, h azy and lacks detail.

3: Has a moderately vivid image of the future self. Can envision some details but much is still unclear.

4: Can envision the future self with considerable vividness and clarity. Has a fairly detailed picture.

5: Has a highly vivid and clear mental image of the future self. Can imagine many specific details.

6: Can picture the future self with extraordinary vividness and detail, almos t like a mental time travel.

Positivity Toward Future Self Rubric: 1: Has strongly negative feelings toward future self.

Actively dislikes or fe ars future self.

2: Feels somewhat negative toward future self. Has doubts, concerns, and expe cts to dislike future self.

3: Has mixed or ambivalent feelings. Feels somewhat positive and somewhat neg ative toward future self.

4: Feels largely positive toward future self. Cares about, has good expectati ons and wants good for future self.

5: Has strongly positive affect toward future self, with feelings of liking, caring and warm regard.

6: Has extremely positive feelings toward future self, with deep fondness, co ncern and sense of kinship.

</rubrics> <output_format> For each assessment, provide: 1.

S5. Discriminant validity

S5. Discriminant validity

S5.1 Expected values for a pure measure

Because questionnaire scores also contain measurement error, the expected neighbor correlation also depends on the reliability of the target questionnaire. At an assumed FSCQ reliability of . 80, a measure of the target construct alone should correlate with the recovery neighbor at about 84% of its target correlation. A neighbor correlation near 100% of the target indicates that the model scores also measure the neighboring construct.

Suppose a model score X reflects true FSC plus independent error, and relates to the RESST only through true FSC. Let ρ be the proportion of FSCQ variance that is construct variance (internal consistency is an upper bound), and let 𝑟 𝐹𝑅 be the observed correlation between the FSCQ and the RESST (.671). Then

Expectations use each configuration's own convergent correlation and are averaged within group. ρ = .80 ρ = .85 ρ = .90 ρ = .95 Observed Open-weight (k = 7): difference +.064 +.084 +.102 +.117 -.014 Open-weight: neighbor partial .100 .071 .044 .021 .219 Frontier (k = 6): difference +.088 +.114 +.138 +.160 +.117 Frontier: neighbor partial .147 .104 .065 .031 .100

The reference value is ρ = .80 (Han et al., 2025, full-scale α = .81). At ρ = .90 or above the frontier group's observed difference falls below the expectation, so the frontier scores are consistent with a pure measure at the reference value and not at every reliability.

Software, precision, reasoning, and cost S6.1 Main-study software setup One NVIDIA A100 (40 GB) rented through Google Colab; Ollama 0.32.4 to 0.32.5 installed each session from the official script; native /api/chat endpoint; temperature 1.0; think: false except for the reasoning-tuned and thinking-mode variants; num_ctx 32,768; one request at a time; no retries. Every response's prompt-token count was logged and compared with a minimum to detect truncation; none occurred in any analyzed configuration. Requests issued under this setup: 6,720 in Study 1 (30 configurations × 224 transcripts) and 1,312 in Study 2 (8 configurations × 164). The extension study issued 1,148 (7 scoring passes × 164).

Frontier scoring software. The frontier scores of Study 1 were reused from Sokol et al. (2026).

Those scores were produced in Claude Code, the provider's agentic command-line tool, with one transcript per new session and only the rubric file. The tool uses its own system prompt and default sampling settings.

S6.2 Marketplace comparison

Nine open-weight models were also scored through a commercial marketplace (OpenRouter) that routes each request to one of several third-party hosts. Requests were restricted to hosts with a no-retention policy; the host was recorded per request; precision was whatever the host used.

Across the nine models the slope of Fisher z on log₁₀ active parameters was 0.009 (SE = 0.048, p = .855), against 0.255 under the controlled software setup.

S6.5 Cost

Open-weight models through the marketplace: $0.0012 per transcript, metered. Frontier: approximately $0.05 per transcript is an estimate for a single request containing rubric and transcript at the provider's published batch rates. The frontier scores in this paper were produced in Claude Code sessions on a subscription account and were not billed per transcript; at list prices these sessions, which also included the tool's system prompt, tool definitions, and file reads, would have cost $0.48 to $1.75 per transcript.

S7. Extension study S7.1 Hardware and bridge criteria

The bridge criteria were fixed before any score from the new hardware existed. For each bridge model, the GX10 environment was treated as equivalent to the A100 when (a) the correlation between pass a and the A100 scores was no more than .05 below the correlation between passes a and b; (b) the convergent correlation from pass a was within .05 of the A100 value; and (c) format failures differed by no more than three. Otherwise the GX10 cells were to be reported separately and not pooled with the A100 cells.

Hardware: ASUS Ascent GX10 (NVIDIA GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip, 128 GB LPDDR5x unified memory per the manufacturer's specification, CUDA 13 runtime), Ollama 0.32.5 in user space, four concurrent requests (two for Llama 3.3 70B), pass a unseeded and pass b seeded (20260730). Model selection rule for large models: instruction-tuned, available at Q4_K_M, weights of about 90 GB or less, context of 32,768 or more; priority to the largest release in each family already studied, then Llama 3.3 70B, then other families.

Model tags. Gemma 4 31B (gemma4:31b; 31.3B active parameters, Q4_K_M). Llama 3.3 70B (llama3.3:70b; a dense 70.6-billion-parameter model, Q4_K_M).

Low et al. (2026), for example, proposed a broader framework for text psychometrics and demonstrated an additional test of content validity based on whether models detect expertidentified prototypical expressions of a construct. Their approach tests whether the model captures the range of expressions associated with a construct, whereas our discriminant comparisons test whether a model's scores correlate more strongly with the target questionnaire than with neighboring ones. Criterion performance alone does not establish either that a model captures the content of a construct or that its scores are specific to that construct. Both forms of evidence are informative, but neither substitutes for the other. Other properties, particularly fairness and generalizability across populations and interview settings, may require additional tests depending on the intended use.

Study 1: results by configuration Criterion: RESST total (1 to 5). One row per participant (first recording); up to 149 participants.Role: standard = the 19 configurations used in the size analyses; precision, reasoning = variants that change a second factor; below-minimum case = below the pre-set minimum of 150 scorable transcripts. Bias = mean model score minus mean RESST. LoA = 95% limits of agreement. Bias² share = bias² / (bias² + SD²). Prop. slope = slope of differences on means. >1 pt = percentage of participants whose two scores differ by more than one point. Scored /224 = transcripts with a usable score on the first attempt. Rescore r = correlation between two complete scoring passes, over every transcript both passes scored (up to 224); the main text uses the first-recording sample (up to 149), which gives .676 and .957 for Granite 4 3B and Gemma 4 31B.
